Bridge protocol v1

The Amthal Portal SDK does not screen-scrape a web page. It runs a typed, versioned message protocol between your native shell and the Client Portal inside the WebView: the shell hands over credentials, locale, theme and font scale; the portal hands back lifecycle events, submissions, navigation and file requests. This page is the reader's edition of the normative specification in bridge/SPEC.md, whose canonical type definitions live in bridge/src/protocol.ts.

You do not have to implement any of this to ship an integration — the React Native, Expo, iOS and Android wrappers already do. Read it when you are debugging a session that never becomes ready, when you need to know exactly what a callback is reporting, or when you are writing a host for a runtime we do not ship yet.

1. The envelope

Every message, in both directions, is a single JSON object with the same five-field shape. There is no second framing, no binary channel and no side band.

{
  "v": 1,
  "id": "<unique-string>",
  "replyTo": "<id of the request this answers, optional>",
  "type": "<message type>",
  "payload": { }
}
  • v must be 1. Every receiver compares it with strict equality and silently ignores anything else — an envelope from a different protocol version is never an error, it simply does not exist.
  • id is unique per sender per session (a UUID v4 or equivalent).
  • replyTo correlates an answer with its request. A message that carries replyTo is never itself replied to.
  • An unknown type is ignored, and unknown payload fields are ignored. That is what makes new optional messages and new optional fields additive: an older host and a newer portal keep working.
  • Input that is not valid JSON is dropped without a diagnostic — the web shim parses defensively because anything on the page could post to the same hook.

Backwards compatibility rule. Additive changes — a new optional message type, a new optional payload field — stay inside protocol 1. A breaking change bumps the protocol version, and the portal and the SDKs must each support {N, N−1} for one release cycle.

2. Transport

Web → native

The web shim (bridge/src/web.ts) probes the following hooks in order and uses the first one present. The presence of any hook is what tells the portal it is embedded; with no hook it behaves as an ordinary browser page and this protocol does not apply.

HookHost
window.__amthalAndroid.postMessage(json) Android — an addJavascriptInterface object named __amthalAndroid
window.webkit.messageHandlers.amthal.postMessage(json) iOS — a WKScriptMessageHandler named amthal
window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(json)
only if window.__AMTHAL_EMBEDDED_RN__ === true		 React Native — react-native-webview

The React Native flag is set through injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded, deliberately: without it the portal would mistake any arbitrary RN WebView that happens to expose ReactNativeWebView for an Amthal host and start handing it lifecycle messages.

Native → web

The native side serializes the envelope to a JSON string S, then evaluates a call whose single argument is S JSON-encoded again:

// envelope  ->  S = {"v":1,"id":"…","type":"init","payload":{…}}
window.__amthalReceive("{\"v\":1,\"id\":\"…\",\"type\":\"init\",\"payload\":{…}}")

The double encoding is not an accident and must not be "simplified": it is what guarantees correct escaping of quotes, newlines and non-BMP characters on every platform's JavaScript evaluation API.

Natives inject their hooks before page content loads — a WKUserScript at .atDocumentStart, addJavascriptInterface before loadUrl, injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded. The shim buffers inbound messages that arrive before the Angular listeners attach, so a host may answer hello with init immediately, with no further synchronisation.

3. The handshake — hello → init → ready

A session becomes usable in three messages, preceded by two things the native side does on its own: the manifest fetch and the version gate. Each step below is a thing that can fail, and the error code it fails with is named.

  1. 1

    Native GET {baseUrl}/embed/manifest.json

    Unauthenticated, before any route is loaded. {baseUrl} includes the portal's deploy path prefix — the manifest is never fetched from the bare origin. Failure ⇒ manifestFailed (or offline when the device has no connectivity).

  2. 2

    Native version gate

    Three comparisons against the manifest (§6). Any failure ⇒ versionIncompatible, and nothing is loaded.

  3. 3

    Native load {baseUrl} + requestToPath(request)

    The URL is the request: which form, which product, read-only or not. It never carries a token, a branch id or any other credential. Load failure ⇒ loadFailed, a non-2xx main frame ⇒ httpError.

  4. 4

    Portal → native hello { protocolVersion, portalVersion }

    Sent by the shim as early as possible — before Angular resolves a route — and re-sent every 10 s until init arrives. If no hello reaches the host within 15 s of the page finishing load, the host raises bridgeTimeout.

  5. 5

    Native → portal init { sdkVersion, platform, protocolVersion, configure, auth, formDelegation? }  (replyTo: the hello id)

    Every hello is answered. init is idempotent — the portal applies the latest one it received, so answering a retry costs nothing.

  6. 6

    Portal apply configure, seed auth, resolve the embed route

    The portal must not activate any /embed/* route before init is applied; it shows its own minimal loading state until then, underneath the SDK's splash.

  7. 7

    Portal → native ready { portalVersion, protocolVersion }

    Exactly once per page load, after the first embed route resolves. The host hides its skeleton and surfaces this to your app — onReady (React Native / Expo), portalReady(portalVersion:) (iOS), onPortalReady(portalVersion) (Android).

  8. 8

    Session active

    From here the traffic is event-driven: submissions, navigation, external links, downloads, back presses, dismiss guards, auth refreshes — all listed in §4.

Auth refresh, mid-session

When the portal's own token refresh fails it does not log the user out and it does not close. It sends authExpired and pauses behind an interstitial until the host hands it a fresh token.

  1. 1

    Portal → native authExpired { reason? }

    The portal pauses. Every SDK puts a "session expired" overlay up at this point.

  2. 2

    Your app obtain a fresh token, then call the SDK

    refresh(auth) from onAuthExpired or ref.updateAuth(auth) (React Native — the same code path), session.updateAuth(auth) (Expo), controller.updateAuth(_:) (iOS), updateAuth(auth) on the view, fragment or activity (Android).

  3. 3

    Native → portal auth { token, branchId?, user? }

    The portal acknowledges with ack { ok } and resumes, retrying the failed request where that is feasible. The overlay clears on the ack — or on a 10 s round-trip timeout, so a portal that never answers cannot strand the user behind a spinner.

The host must have somewhere to get a token from. The SDK never talks to your authentication API and cannot refresh anything by itself. If you do not wire a refresh path, the session stays paused: React Native falls back to onError({ code: 'authExpired' }) when no onAuthExpired prop is given, iOS reports it through portalError as well as the overlay, Expo routes it to its onAuthExpired event only, and Android moves the view into its error state.

Teardown

The host sends destroy, waits up to 1 s for an ack (best effort), then releases the WebView. The portal clears its persisted auth (USER_KEY, BRANCH_ID) on destroy whether or not the ack is delivered, and the native side clears WebView storage for the portal origin.

4. Message catalogue

Portal → native

TypePayloadMeaning and host obligation
helloHelloPayload First message once the shim boots. The host must answer with init; re-sent every 10 s until it does.
readyReadyPayload Angular booted, auth applied, first embed route resolved. Once per page load. Hide your skeleton here.
authExpiredAuthExpiredPayload Token refresh failed inside the portal. Send a fresh auth (§3).
formSubmittedFormSubmittedPayload A submission succeeded. The SDK never auto-closes — your app decides what happens next (thank-you screen, dismiss, navigate to history).
formCancelled— The user left through the form's own close/finish affordance.
navigateNavigatePayload Informational; fired on every router navigation inside /embed/*. Useful for a native title bar or analytics.
openExternalOpenExternalPayload Open outside the WebView — system browser, SFSafariViewController, Custom Tabs — unless your handler intercepts it.
downloadRequestDownloadRequestPayload Download the URL with the supplied headers attached and present it natively (QuickLook / ACTION_VIEW). Header values must never be logged.
formOpFormOpRequestPayload A delegated form data operation. Only sent when init.formDelegation === true (§9).
hapticHapticPayload Optional feedback cue; a host may ignore it. Implemented on iOS; ignored on Android.
logLogPayload Diagnostics. Hosts must drop these in release builds.
ackAckPayload or a typed reply Answer to a host request; always carries replyTo.

Native → portal

TypePayloadMeaning and reply
initInitPayload Reply to hello. Idempotent — the portal applies the most recent one.
authAuthPayload (Re)issue credentials at any time. The portal acks.
configureConfigurePayload Apply locale, theme or font scale at runtime. Switching to 'ar' also flips the document to dir=rtl.
backPressed— Android hardware back. The portal replies BackHandledPayload: {handled:true} means the web consumed it (e.g. stepped back a form step), {handled:false} means the host should close. A timeout is treated as {handled:false}.
dismissRequested— iOS swipe-dismiss / ✕ guard. The portal replies DismissStatePayload: {dirty:true} means the host should show a confirm-discard prompt. A timeout is treated as {dirty:false}.
destroy— Teardown. The portal clears persisted auth; the host waits ≤1 s for the ack, then releases the WebView.
ackAckPayload Generic acknowledgement; always carries replyTo.

Why backPressed and dismissRequested are questions, not commands. A multi-step form has its own idea of "back", and a half-filled form has unsaved work. Both messages ask the portal first and fall back to the safe native behaviour on timeout, so the user is never trapped by a web layer that stopped answering.

5. Payload shapes

These are the canonical TypeScript definitions from bridge/src/protocol.ts. The Swift and Kotlin SDKs mirror them exactly; where the naming differs on a native surface it is noted underneath.

export type PortalLocale = 'en' | 'ar';
export type PortalTheme  = 'light' | 'dark' | 'system';
export type HostPlatform = 'ios' | 'android' | 'react-native' | 'flutter';

interface ConfigurePayload {
  locale?: PortalLocale;
  theme?: PortalTheme;
  fontScale?: number;            // 1.0 = the portal's default
}

interface AuthPayload {
  token: string;                 // backend bearer token
  branchId?: string | null;
  user?: unknown;                // optional pre-built portal user object
}

interface HelloPayload { protocolVersion: number; portalVersion: string; }
interface ReadyPayload { portalVersion: string; protocolVersion: number; }

interface InitPayload {
  sdkVersion: string;
  platform: HostPlatform;
  protocolVersion: number;
  configure: ConfigurePayload;
  auth: AuthPayload;
  formDelegation?: boolean;      // see §9
}

interface AuthExpiredPayload { reason?: string; }

interface FormSubmittedPayload {
  productID: number;
  applicationNo?: number | string;
  batchID?: number | string;
  headerID?: number | string;
  raw?: unknown;                 // opaque passthrough
}

interface NavigatePayload      { path: string; title?: string; }
interface OpenExternalPayload  { url: string; }

interface DownloadRequestPayload {
  url: string;
  filename?: string;
  mime?: string;
  headers?: Record<string, string>;   // e.g. Authorization — attach, never log
}

interface HapticPayload { style: 'light' | 'medium' | 'heavy' | 'success' | 'error'; }
interface LogPayload    { level: 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'; message: string; data?: unknown; }

interface BackHandledPayload  { handled: boolean; }   // ack to backPressed
interface DismissStatePayload { dirty: boolean; }     // ack to dismissRequested
interface AckPayload          { ok: boolean; error?: string; }

Anonymous sessions: omit auth, never send an empty token. On React Native, leaving the auth prop off produces an init with no auth key at all — that absence is how the portal is told it is on the public plane and made to drop stored credentials. Sending { token: '' } instead is an authenticated session with a broken token and behaves differently.

Two naming splits are worth knowing before you debug a payload by eye: the optional user object is user in TypeScript, userJSON in Swift and userJson in Kotlin (the native sides take it as an already-serialized JSON string); and the Expo wrapper stringifies user into userJSON before it crosses into native code.

6. Manifest and the version gate

Before loading any route the SDK fetches, without authentication:

GET {baseUrl}/embed/manifest.json

{ "portalVersion": "1.8.0", "bridgeProtocolVersion": 1, "minSdkVersion": "1.0.0" }

Three gates run against it. Any failure raises versionIncompatible and nothing is loaded; a network failure instead raises manifestFailed (or offline when there is no connectivity at all).

GateRuleWhat it protects against
ProtocolbridgeProtocolVersion must equal a protocol version the SDK implements — today, exactly 1A portal upgraded across a breaking protocol change talking to an app that cannot be updated.
Portal floorportalVersion ≥ your minPortalVersion, when you set oneA tenant still running an older portal than the one your release was tested against.
SDK floorThe SDK's own version ≥ the manifest's minSdkVersion, when presentAn old app build against a portal that now requires newer host behaviour.

The manifest is fetched relative to the full base URL, never the bare origin. The portal deploys under a path prefix (<base href="/portal/">), so https://portal.example.com/portal is a correct baseUrl and https://portal.example.com is not. Check it from a terminal before you blame the SDK:

curl -sI https://portal.example.com/portal/embed/manifest.json

A content-type: application/json is what you want. text/html means the SPA catch-all served index.html — the request never reached a real manifest — and the session will fail with manifestFailed.

Setting minPortalVersion is the deliberate way to make an incompatibility visible: catch versionIncompatible in your error handler and show "please update the app" rather than a blank form.

7. Timeouts

Every timeout in the protocol is a constant in TIMINGS, shared by all four hosts. They are normative: a host that waits longer hangs the user, one that waits less will fail on a slow network.

ConstantValueWho waits, and what happens on expiry
helloTimeoutMs15 000 ms The host, after the page finishes loading. No hello ⇒ bridgeTimeout.
initTimeoutMs10 000 ms The portal, after sending hello. No init ⇒ it re-sends hello and keeps waiting.
requestTimeoutMs10 000 ms Default for any request/ack round trip — auth, backPressed, dismissRequested. On expiry the host applies the safe default (handled:false, dirty:false, clear the refresh overlay).
formOpTimeoutMs20 000 ms Delegated form reads (§9).
formSubmitTimeoutMs90 000 ms Delegated form writes — validate and submit, which may carry base64 attachments.
destroy ack1 000 ms The host, during teardown. Best effort only: the WebView is released either way.

8. Security rules

These are normative requirements on every host implementation, not recommendations. If you are writing your own host, this section is the part you must not simplify.

Credentials never travel in a URL

Tokens, branch ids and user objects cross only inside init and auth payloads — never in a path, a query string or a fragment. The navigation URL carries the request (form type, product, batch, header, read-only) and nothing else. This keeps credentials out of WebView history, out of server access logs and out of any Referer a page might emit.

Origin and path confinement

  • Main-frame navigation is restricted to the configured portal origin and the basePath + /embed subtree. Anything else is cancelled and routed through the openExternal path instead — so an in-portal link to a marketing site opens in the system browser rather than replacing your embedded form.
  • Path checks use the deployment's real base path, never a literal /embed prefix. The shared helpers basePathOf() and isEmbedPath() exist so that no host re-implements this comparison and gets it wrong.
  • Before dispatching any inbound message, and before every native→web evaluation, the host verifies that the WebView's current URL origin is still the configured portal origin.

The most common integration failure lives in this rule. Confinement is computed as basePath + '/embed'. If you configure baseUrl without the portal's deploy prefix, basePath is empty, the portal's very first in-app navigation looks like it is outside the subtree, and the user is thrown into the system browser instead of the form. The symptom looks like a routing bug; the cause is one missing path segment.

Transport

  • HTTPS only. An http: base URL is rejected at config time, with a loopback exception for development (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, and 10.0.2.2 on the Android emulator). The escape hatch for a non-loopback plain-HTTP dev portal is build-gated on every platform — __DEV__, #if DEBUG, FLAG_DEBUGGABLE — so it is inert in a release build.
  • Android: file-access flags off, mixed content never allowed. iOS: no link preview on the form view.

Data at rest and in logs

  • On destroy — and on host-app logout — the portal clears its persisted auth (USER_KEY, BRANCH_ID) and the host clears WebView storage for the portal origin.
  • downloadRequest.headers may contain an Authorization value. Attach it to the request; never write it to a log.
  • log messages from the portal are dropped in release builds, and the SDKs' own enableLogging flag is honoured only in debug builds.
  • Store the token your app hands to auth in the Keychain, the Android Keystore or expo-secure-store — never in plain async storage, a file or a log line.

9. Form delegation — when the host owns the data plane

By default the portal calls its own HTTP endpoints for form data: it is a customer-plane application with a customer token. Some hosts cannot work that way — a back-office app whose staff identity must hit the internal /DMS/Forms/* endpoints, with per-login pre-entrance checks the portal must not know about. Form delegation is the additive protocol 1 capability for exactly that case: the portal becomes a pure renderer and every data operation crosses the bridge.

Only the React Native wrapper implements form delegation. It is not available on iOS, Android or the Expo sheet. The Expo wrapper fails fast if you pass onFormOp: it reports onError({ code: 'loadFailed', … }) and returns a no-op session rather than presenting a sheet that would silently render nothing.

  • The host opts in by sending formDelegation: true in init. In React Native that flag is derived purely from the presence of an onFormOp prop.
  • While delegation is active the portal must not call its own form HTTP endpoints inside /embed/*, and must not fall back to them on a timeout — a delegated session that fails surfaces a load/submit error rather than quietly using the wrong identity.
  • params carries route and product values only (productID, batchID, headerID, workflowDetailID, isEdit, …). The portal never sends identity — no user id, no token, no branch. The host owns identity and augments the call.
  • Multipart bodies cross as ordered entries. The host must rebuild the body preserving entry order and duplicate keys; a map would lose both.
  • A reply with status: 401 makes the portal run its embedded auth-expired flow, i.e. it sends authExpired and waits for a fresh auth.
type FormOp =
  | 'getCategories'
  | 'getFormSchema'          // whole render shape in one call — there is no second templates call
  | 'getFormFields'
  | 'validateForm'
  | 'submitForm'
  | 'getWorkflowDetails'
  | 'submitFinalApproval'
  | 'submitForApproval';

type SerializedFormEntry =
  | { key: string; value: string }
  | { key: string; file: { name: string; type: string; dataBase64: string } };

interface FormOpRequestPayload {
  op: FormOp;
  params: Record<string, string>;
  entries?: SerializedFormEntry[];   // validateForm / submitForm
  body?: unknown;                    // JSON ops (submitForApproval)
}

interface FormOpResponsePayload {
  ok: boolean;
  body?: unknown;    // the raw response body the portal's HTTP client would have parsed
  error?: string;    // human-readable, surfaced in the portal UI when ok=false
  status?: number;   // 401 triggers the auth-expired flow
}

On the React Native side this is one async prop: onFormOp(request) => Promise<unknown>. Resolve it with the response body; throw to signal failure.

10. Testing the bridge

Drive the embed routes from a desktop browser

A -dev portal build ships a mock native host, so you can exercise the embedded plane — the same routes, the same init payload shape — without building an app. Every value the real host would send is a query parameter:

{baseUrl}/embed/form/external/{productID}?mockEmbed=1
{baseUrl}/embed/form/internal/{productID}?mockEmbed=1&mockToken=<jwt>&mockBranch=12

# optional, in any combination
&mockLocale=ar   &mockTheme=dark   &mockFontScale=1.2
&mockPlatform=ios|android|react-native

The default is deliberately anonymous: with no mockToken the mock host sends an init that carries no auth, which is the public plane exactly as a real anonymous session sees it. mockPlatform changes which transport hint the portal believes it is running under, which is how you reproduce a platform-specific rendering difference from a laptop.

Conformance

A host implementation is conformant when it passes the scripted sequences in bridge/conformance/: the handshake happy path, hello-retry, the auth-expiry round trip, both answers to a back press, both answers to the dismiss guard, destroy teardown, unknown-type ignore, wrong-v ignore, and origin-violation drop. MockNativeHost (bridge/src/mock.ts) drives the web side; a static portal build plus scripted pages drive the native side.

Reading a failed session

The error code tells you which stage of §3 broke: manifestFailed and versionIncompatible happen before anything is loaded; loadFailed, httpError and offline are the page load itself; bridgeTimeout means the page loaded but the shim never spoke, which almost always means the URL was not an /embed/* route on a portal build that ships the shim. Each code, with its per-platform triggers, is listed on the Troubleshooting page.

Changing the protocol. bridge/src/protocol.ts is the single source of truth and every native implementation mirrors its shapes exactly. Any change to it is a protocol change and requires a SPEC.md pull request first — spec, then code, then the four hosts.
